ho_0148d78b4bb7.scope: In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.

ho_063599568446.description: Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

Emphasis on spectroscopic techniques such as UV Visible, infrared, NMR (1H, 13C and other elements, NOE, correlation spectroscopies), ESR, atomic absorption and emission, photoelectron, Mössbauer, and fluorescence. ho_0bf2b4156656.scope: The fundamentals of supply chain – concepts course is aimed at providing a solid grounding and understanding of what constitutes a supply chain, setting the stage for more advanced topics. The course provides students with the opportunity to get clarity and insights into the various key components and concepts of the supply chain. This course will assist in understanding Supply Chain Management (SCM) not as a technology but rather a business strategy tool for the companies trying to create competitive advantage in the market. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: • Attain familiarity with the fundamental concepts of the SCM and its use in organizations. • Understand the key components of the Supply Chain and the interrelationships. • Importance of supply chain in today’s business environment and the impact of Globalization. • Supply Chain emerging trends
ho_0bf2b4156656.syllabus_text: Topic Contents What is Supply Chain Management & how does it create Value? Describe the cycle and push/ pull view of a supply chain. Identify the key supply chain decision phases. Goal of supply chain & impact of supply chain decision on the success of a firm Strategic Fit & Scope Achieving strategic fit is critical to a company’s overall success. Supply Chain Drivers and Metrics Identify the major drivers of supply chain performance. Discuss the role each driver plays. Describe the major obstacles that must be overcome to manage a supply chain successfully. Designing the distribution network Designing the distribution network in a supply chain, Network design in the supply chain, Network design in uncertain environment Key components/ operations of the Supply Chain – Overview Key components of the supply chain-overview, objectives and key concepts and its relationships with upstream and downstream components –Overview of SCOR model, Product Lifecycle Management, Revenue and Pricing, Order Management, Production/manufacturing, Maintenance, Quality, Procurement, inventory, warehousing, transportation, demand and supply planning, cost management etc. Key Supply Chain Management Processes All the key supply chain process flows or modern best practices – Source to Pay/Procure to Pay, Production Order to Costing, design to release, Order Fulfilment and ATP/CTP, Inbound Shipment to Delivery, Outbound Shipment to Delivery, Freight Invoice to Approval, Warehouse Receiving-storage-picking and shipping, Transportation, E-Commerce Supply Chain E-commerce is transforming supply chains, boosting demand for automation, real- time logistics, and omni-channel fulfilment. Also covers topics on warehousing and inventory management, last-mile delivery, and customer experience. Also understand how technology shaping commerce logistics – alerts, telemetry, shipment visibility tracking Supply Chain and Globalization Supply Chain and Global SCM Excellence, Strategic alliances, Global logistics, Customer value, Product Strategy and Customer Segmentation, Impact of globalization/de-globalization on Supply chain. Changing dynamics of global commerce. Digital Supply Chain Industry 1.0 to 5.0 evolution. AI and Automation in Supply Chains – how machine learning and AI are revolutionizing supply chain operations. Gain insights into predictive analytics, demand forecasting and AI-Powered decision making to optimize and make process efficient and reduce costs. Blockchain and RFID in Supply Chains. Cloud-Based Supply Chain Solutions. Major Supply Chain Applications and Technologies What are various SCM Applications (e-Procurement, TMS, WMS etc.)– best of the breed and IT application vendors. Key features and functionalities of the applications and how they interrelate / interact with each other process-wise. Major Integration touchpoints and common middleware technologies and tools used for driving interoperability (Digital Integration). Gartner - magic quadrant ratings of some of the supply chain applications. Supply Chain Risk Management Identifying risks and building resilience in the supply chain. Supply Chain emerging trends and using tools to create competitive advantage Gen AI use cases in Supply Chain, Types of Supply Chain Analytics – over view on predictive and prescriptive, Sustainability and Circular economy etc. Key SCM analytics applications – overview. ho_0e07824205ae.scope: The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.

ho_137479dd5d31.description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

ho_137479dd5d31.scope: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.

ho_174f7d34dbd9.description: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.

ho_174f7d34dbd9.scope: The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system.

ho_17be65718433.description: This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.

Currently, with the advances in computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to study material properties for various applications. ho_1a8f83f8530b.description: Software engineering is a discipline that allows us to apply engineering and computer science con- cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. There are several areas to focus on within software engineering, such as requirement specification, de- sign, development, testing, maintenance and project management. The course is designed to present software engineering concepts and principles in parallel with the software development life cycle.

ho_1afe4463f400.scope: This course develops a comprehensive understanding of computer architecture and organization, from quantifying processor performance to designing a working processor and its supporting memory system. It begins with performance measurement and comparison using key metrics, benchmarking tools, and Amdahl's law. Building on this, it covers the MIPS architecture and instruction set. The course then examines the design of single-cycle and multi-cycle processor. It further explores pipelined processor design, the handling of structural, data, and control hazards through forwarding, stalling, reordering, and branch prediction techniques. The memory hierarchy is studied to exploit locality of reference, covering memory technologies, cache mapping functions, cache controller design, cache performance metrics, and multi-level caches. Finally, the course introduces advanced techniques for increasing instruction-level parallelism, including multiple issue, loop unrolling, speculation, and dynamic scheduling. TEXT BOOKS (T1) Patterson, David A & J L Hennenssy, Computer Organisation & Design, Elsevier, 6th Ed., 2021. (T2) Samir Palnitkar, Verilog HDL: A Guide to Digital Design and Synthesis, Pearson Education Asia, 2nd Ed. 2006. REFERENCE BOOK (R1) J.L. Hennessy & D.A. Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach, Morgan Kauffmann, 6th Ed, 2019. Students will gain hands-on experience with Python programming fundamentals, including program structure, data types, variables, and expressions. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. ho_1ced5e96a559.description: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: ▪ Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses. ▪ Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination. ▪ Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction. ▪ Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 ▪ Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations. ▪ Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods. ▪ Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks. ▪ Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications. ▪ Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data. ▪ Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software. ho_1d321ef36b48.scope: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical aspects of pharmaceutical engineering, with a focus on key unit operations involved in the development and manufacturing of pharmaceutical formulations. It covers a wide range of processes including size reduction and separation, drying, evaporation, distillation, mixing, filtration, centrifugation, extraction, compression, crystallization, and materials of plant construction. The course emphasizes the selection, operation, and application of various equipment used in the pharmaceutical industry.

ho_1f201255f0c7.description: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames. Scope & Objectives: To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity. Course learning outcomes:  Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.  Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.  Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.  Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects. Text Books: T1. H. Goldstein, C. Poole, and J. Safko, Classical Mechanics, Third Edition, Pearson Edu. Inc., 2002. T2. N. C. Rana and P. S. Joag, Classical Mechanics, McGraw Hill, First Edition, 2008. Reference Books:  L. D. Landau and E. M. Lifshitz, Mechanics, Third Edition, Butterworth-Heinemann, 2000.  L. N. Hand and J. D. ho_1f201255f0c7.syllabus_text: T1 ==>Text Book-1, T2 ==> Text Book-2, CN ==> Class Notes Lecture Learning Objectives Topics Learning Outcome Ref. 0 A Few mathematical tools Vector Algebra: Basic Operations, Differential Operators (Gradient, divergence, curl, and Laplacian) in curvilinear coordinate systems, Multivariable Calculus (total derivatives and chain rule) Apply vector algebra, differential operators in curvilinear coordinate systems, and multivariable calculus to formulate and solve problems in classical mechanics. CN (Self revision) 1 Kinematics & dynamics of a mechanical system in Newtonian approach: A very brief overview Newtonian mechanics for a particle/system of particles: Conservation principles, etc. Recall the fundamental concepts of Newtonian kinematics and dynamics relevant to analytical mechanics. T1: 1.1 - 1.2 (Self revision), CN 2-3 Newtonian approach: A Critical analysis Constrained Motions: Classification of constraints. Degree of freedom (DOF), generalized coordinates. Determine the degrees of freedom of mechanical systems, and formulate their motion using generalized coordinates. T1: 1.3 T2: 1.1- 1.2, 2.2, 2.3 and CN 4-6 Lagrangian Formulation (user- friendly packaging): Systematic methods to eliminate/bypass constraints, Principle of virtual work, d’Alembert’s principle (may shock you at first and certainly test your patience!), Euler- Lagrange’s (E-L) equation Learning of alternate approach but more elegant, and most importantly, powerful, compared to Newtonian. T1: 1.4- 1.6 T2: 1.3,1.4, 1.7, 2.1,2.4 7-8 Central force problem: A detailed study Setting up the problem through Lagrangian approach: Reduction of two-body problem to an equivalent one-body problem. Apply the Lagrangian formalism to analyse central-force motion and derive its equations of motion. T1: 3.1 9-12 Qualitative understanding of power law forces: An Effective Potential description Two first integrals of motion, classification of orbits based on bounded/unbounded motion, stability criteria, closure property, etc. Use conservation laws to analyse bounded and unbounded central-force orbits and determine their stability and closure characteristics. T1: 3.2 – 3.3, 3.5- 3.6 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 13-14 Kepler problems: Study to our solar system Orbits under inverse-square law of force, any deviation from inverse square law? Qualitative understanding of precession of orbits via phenomenological model. Analyse orbital motion under the inverse-square law and explain orbital precession arising from deviations from the inverse-square force. T1: 3.7- 3.8 15-17 Calculus of variations (an integral principle approach) and its application to different branches of physics Principle of least action : Fermat’s principle in optics, Geodesics for material bodies, Material bodies in conservative force fields (Brachistochrone, Tautochrone, etc.) Apply the principle of least action to analyse the motion of light and material bodies and solve elementary variational problems. T2: 6.1- 6.4, 7.1- 7.3 18-20 Hamilton’s principle: An elegant & more powerful approach Derivation of the Euler– Lagrange Equations from Hamilton’s principle Establish the connection with D'Alembert's principle. T1: 2.1- 2.5 21 Symmetry principle and conservation laws Derivation of conserved quantities from the symmetries of the Lagrangian Relate symmetries to conservation laws T1: 2.6- 2.7 22-24 Hamiltonian Formulation: A Phase space description Construction of the Hamiltonian from Lagrangian (the Lagrangian's twin sibling!) through duality transformation. Construct the Hamiltonian from the Lagrangian using the Legendre transformation and interpret the dual formulation of classical mechanics. T1: 8.1, 8.2 T2: 5.1- 5.3, 5.5 25-27 Canonical Transformation(CT): Four basic CTs and the corresponding generating functions (GF) Analyse canonical transformations using generating functions T1: 9.1- 9.4 T2: 8.1- 8.5 28-29 Poisson bracket(PB) Poisson bracket and other canonical invariants (where you start sensing quantum mechanics lurking in the background!) Apply PB and canonical invariants to analyse dynamical systems T1: 9.5 and CN 3 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 30-32 Kinematics of Rigid Body Motion Independent Coordinates, Orthogonal Transformations, Formal properties of transformation matrix Analyse rigid-body kinematics using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles. T1: 4.1- 4.3 33-35 Kinematics of Rigid Body Motion Euler Angles, Finite and Infinitesimal Rotations Describe rigid-body orientation using Euler angles and analyse finite and infinitesimal rotations in three- dimensional space. T1: 4.4, 4.7, 4.8 36-39 Motion in Rotating Reference Frames Rate of Change of a vector, Coriolis Effects (hard to avoid when you're sitting in a lecture room on the rotating Earth!) Related to the realistic and physical aspects of earth’s rotation, namely Coriolis effects. ho_232754cc6ccf.description: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design (CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation, and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro- duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative, lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.

ho_24b9a023c823.description: This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.

ho_24b9a023c823.scope: • Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. • Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. • Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. • Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. • Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras.

ho_277a8247ce99.description: The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail.

ho_2965463f7dfe.scope: This is the last one of the four Physical Chemistry courses named for M.Sc. (Hons.) Chemistry Programme. The course mainly covers chemical changes in terms of chemical kinetics, surface and interfacial phenomena, and the associated theories. The objective is to understand the chemical changes and also to be able to connect these changes to structure and equilibrium properties learnt in the previous courses.

ho_2a344cdfeac4.description: This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.

text: Make-up Policy: Permitted at the discretion of the instructor-in-charge, and only in emergencies or significant unforeseen circumstances.

ho_2a344cdfeac4.scope: Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without fundamentally exploitative structures.
ho_2a344cdfeac4.syllabus_text: Class No Lecture Session Reference Learning outcomes 1-4 Why Marxism? An introduction to the many theories and narratives that claim to explain inequality in society. Relevance of Karl Marx in the 21st century. “Why so much Inequality?” – Yanis Varoufakis Critique of Malthusian claims of overpopulation - “Are there just too many of us?” - Manali Chakrabarti “All in the genes?” - Richard Lewontin Here the course begins with key questions about the roots of inequality in modern industrial society and arrives at some answers. Primarily this involves being able to identify gaps and problems in the dominant discourse around inequality. 5-8 Dialectics and Historical Materialism Brief overview of the history of class society from a Marxist perspective and the marxist method of analysis. Modes and relations of production transition from primitive to feudal society and then to industrial capitalism. What is a “Mode of Production”? - Paul Cockshott Agrarian Origins of Capitalism - The Origins of Capitalism by Ellen Meiksins Wood Part 1 - Man’s Worldly Goods - Leo Huberman The History Book – Jannik Hastrup - 1974 Chapter 2 - Structure and Action - Alex Callinicos Here we directly enter the mature theoretical framework which Marx had developed to explain the history of class society and its recurrent feature of social inequality. His critique of Hegel is crucial to understand dialectical materialism. 9-18 Marx’s Labour Theory of Value What creates value? Use Value – Exchange Value – Surplus Value Cooperation & development of Machinery General law of capitalist accumulation Ch 1 & 2, from The Value of Everything: Making and Taking in the Global Economy, by Mariana Mazzucato A Reader’s Guide to Marx’s Capital - Choonara (pages 18-113) Excerpt from Red Rosa – biography of Rosa Luxembourg Here we try to grasp the specific ways in which surplus value is extracted in a capitalist mode of production and the nature of the power relationship embedded therein. 19-21 Fetishism of the Commodity Alienation Marxist Crisis Theories Tendency for Fall in the Rate of Profit Counteracting Factors Mandi – Yashowardhan Mishra (2019) Farmer’s first taste of chocolate The Cause of Depressions - Michael Roberts Counteracting Factors (to TFRP) - Marx One of the major consequences of capitalist social organization is the rise of the commodity form as a dominant form of social metabolism – Fetishism of the commodity and the alienation it produces are quite relevant to understanding many social ills, including in contemporary society. 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 22-26 Critique of Neoclassical and Neoliberal Ideology 1. Free trade 2. Capitalist Efficiency 3. Self-Interest 4. Say’s Law 5. Invisible Hand of the Market 6. Rational Consumer 7. Marginal Utility Strange History of the Economic Agent - by Duncan K Foley Is Free Trade Always the Answer? - Ha Joon Chang Revisiting Inequality through ‘Capitalist Hierarchy’- What do Bosses Do? - Stephen Marglin On the Margins - Foley Certain ideologies pervade modern political and economic thought, some inherited from classical philosophy, some new. Here we examine the origin, essence and validity of these claims/concepts. 27-30 Imperialism Monopoly Capitalism - Why imperialism survives even after decolonization. Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism - VI Lenin The Global Commodity - John Smith Ref; Samir Amin, Baran, Sweezy One of the major consequences of capitalist social organization is the rise of the commodity form as a dominant form of social metabolism – Fetishism of the commodity and the alienation it produces are quite relevant to understanding many social ills, including in contemporary society. 31-36 What is Socialism and Communism? Discussion on Violence Socialism Now - Case Study on China The Communist Manifesto - Marx & Engels (page 31-84) Revolution and the Question of Violence; Ch 2 & 8 – Why Marx Was Right - Terry Eagleton Selected Works of Mao-Tse-Tung (selected paragraphs will be discussed in class) “Excerpts From Talks Given In Wuchang, Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shanghai” - Deng Xiaoping Comprehend class struggle going beyond popular misconceptions and grasp the historical nature of this process. In addition, the aim is to develop clarity in thinking about the history of different forms of violence and its role in the liberation and oppression of people. 37-40 Building Alternatives - Reorganizing work and society Can we democratize work? - “Contradictions of Democracy in a Workers’ Cooperative” – Varman & Chakrabarti How can capitalism be overturned? “What is to be Done” - Lenin Workers Co-ops - Cooperation Jackson Finally, is Marxism relevant today and if so, why? Is it true that capitalism is increasing the median wages of people across the world? Here, we address the modern forms of capitalism and locate how Marx’s ideas continue to hold relevance in theoretically understanding these phenomena and offering a way beyond these systems. 3 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division

The recent development of the subject and its application in the research level will be discussed. Course will assume a basic knowledge of optics at the level of the core Physics courses. The course will also provide theoretical background for the optics experiments done in Electromagnetism & Optics Lab. (PHYF214).
ho_31b6d584775e.syllabus_text: Module No. Learning Objectives Topics to be covered Reference Chapters and Sections Learning outcome 1 Introduction to optics, Fermat's principle. Basic introduction to optics, Newton's corpuscular model, laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat’s Principle and its applications T.B.: 2.1-2.5 To derive laws of reflection & refraction using Fermat's principle. Modern version of Fermat’s Principle and spherical refracting surfaces. Understanding various optical phenomena for example mirage by solving the ray equation, obtain ray paths in inhomogeneous media, transit time calculation in propogating through parabolic index medium. 2 Refraction and Reflection by Spherical Surfaces Basic concepts of Refraction at a Single Spherical Surface, Reflection by a Single Spherical Surface, The Thin Lens, The Principle Foci and Focal Lengths of a Lens, The Newton Formula, Lateral Magnification T.B: 3.1-3.7 To describe the image formation at spherical surface and to learn the formation of paraxial image by thin lens. 3 Matrix methods in paraxial optics. Matrices for translation, refraction and reflection, unit planes, nodal points, system of two thin lenses. T.B.: 4.1 – 4.5 Using the matrix method one calculate the effect of translation and refraction on paraxial rays. One can obtain the position of nodal points in an optical system and analyze the combination of lenses. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 4 Aberrations Chromatic aberration, monochromatic aberrations, distortion T.B.: 5.1-5.4 To understand that chromatic aberration and monochromatic aberrations. 5 Origin of refractive index. Origin of refractive index; Dispersion: normal and anomalous dispersion. Rayleigh Scattering T.B.: 6.5-6.6 To understand the origin of refractive index and describe the phenomenon of Rayleigh scattering 6 Group velocity and pulse dispersion Group velocity of a wave packet; propagation in a non- dispersive and dispersive medium. T.B.: 11.1- 11.3 To explain the concept of group velocity, illustrate the group velocity of a wave packet using Gaussian pulse. To understand propagation in a dispersive and a non- dispersive medium. 7 Two beam interference by division of wavefront. Interference of light waves, intensity distribution, Fresnel biprism. Displacement of fringes. T.B.: 13.4- 13.12 To understand the interference pattern, the intensity distribution are the foundations to the applications e.g. Fresnel biprism. Displacement of fringes, phase change on reflection. 8 Interference by division of amplitude Interference by a plane parallel film, reflecting non- films, colors of thin films, Newton’s rings T.B.: 14.1- 14.4, 14.10- 14.11 To understand thin film interference; to explain formation of Newton’s rings, working of Michelson Interferometer 9 Coherence Temporal coherence and line width, spatial coherence. T.B.: 17.1- 17.4 To define and hence estimate coherence time and coherence length of a given source, estimate the monochromaticity or the spectral purity of source, concept of spatial coherence. 10 Fraunhofer Diffraction I Fraunhofer diffraction: Single slit, double-slit, N- slit diffraction pattern, diffraction grating T.B.: 17.1- 17.3, 17.6 - 17.8 Fraunhofer diffraction by single slit and double slit, a student will be able to apply the concept of N slit diffraction to understand the working principle of grating and dispersion power of grating, its applications. 11 Fresnel Diffraction Fresnel diffraction: Fresnel half- period zones, the zone - plate T.B.: 19.1-19.3 To analyze Fresnel half-period zones and its applications. 12 Polarization and double refraction. Malus and Brewster’s laws, double refraction, optical activity, linearly and circularly polarized light, Jones calculus. T.B: 21.1- 21.7, 21.14- 21.15 To learn to produce various forms of polarized light waves; how to control polarization of EM waves at interfaces with various angles of incidence, concept of Brewster angle and its importance in various applications, Jones calculus, Faraday rotation. 13 Laser: An Introduction Spontaneous emission, Stimulated emission, Einstein coefficients, threshold condition, some laser systems. ho_33fd7f501df1.scope: A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. ho_363b80a3ae60.description: This course introduces the principles, design, and applications of optoelectronic devices. The course begins with a description of the interaction of light with semiconductor materials in a p-n junction configuration. This includes the phenomena of absorption, electroluminescence, and stimulated emission. The distinction between direct and indirect semiconductor materials is noted. Basic devices are then described: photodiodes, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), semiconductor optical amplifiers, and laser diodes. Array detectors, including complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) and charge-coupled devices (CCD) arrays, and array LEDs are then introduced. Basic specifications and applications of each of these devices are described, including solar cells, imaging with array detectors, and LED displays. II. Textbooks and References: TB1: Optoelectronics and Photonics: Principles and Practices (2nd Edition) by S.O. Kasap. R1: Solid State Electronic Devices by Ben Streetman & Sanjay Banerjee. R2: Semiconductor Optoelectronic Devices by Pallab Bhattacharya. III. Course Objectives: • Understand the fundamental solid-state physics governing light-matter interactions in semiconductor materials. • Analyze the operation, design parameters, and performance metrics of modern optoelectronic emitters (LEDs, Lasers) and detectors (Photodiodes, Solar Cells). • Evaluate the engineering principles behind advanced display architectures, flexible electronics, and matrix-based image sensors. • Apply theoretical knowledge through hands-on computational modeling and simulation of optoelectronic device behavior. Scope and Objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: a. Understand and apply prompt engineering techniques to control the behavior of LLMs. b. Build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines for combining LLMs with external knowledge bases. c. Fine-tune LLMs for specific tasks using publicly available models. d. Leverage tool calling to enable LLMs to interact with external systems and APIs. e. Design and implement multi-agent workflows where multiple LLMs interact to solve complex tasks. f. Implement guardrails to ensure the safe and ethical deployment of LLMs in production environments. g. Understand the internal architecture of LLMs and the entire life cycle of LLM Training and Fine-Tuning. h. ho_3acf691e67c2.description: This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course.

ho_3baa6ccfa842.description: Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure.

ho_3cb35dd8e608.scope: Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states. Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.

ho_3f2347d3411f.description: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is based on the idea where we learn by interacting with our environment. It is a collection of machine learning techniques where agent(s) learn how to behave in an environment by performing actions and assessing the results. RL approach is building programs that learn how to predict and act in stochastic environment, based on experience. This course will provide an overview to students on some of the fundamental ideas on which modern RL is built including Markov decision processes, Mult-armed bandits value functions, Monte Carlo estimation, dynamic programming, TD methods, approximation methods, Actor-Critic methods, etc. This course will help students to understand and apply RL in several systems including video distribution systems, game development, IOT devices, robotics, clinical decision making, industrial process control, finance portfolio balancing, etc.

ho_44fa27c60333.description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.

ho_461a9d9df7d6.scope: This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations, which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical process plants. Fundamentals of this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.

ho_4a95a8851c47.description: The course introduces students to the applications of different techniques of Statistics, Analytics, and machine learning to solve financial problems. The students will be exposed to understanding the characteristics of financial data, solving univariate and multivariate time series based forecasting problems for prices and returns, problems on portfolio allocation, rebalancing and optimization, Security performance analytics, trading strategies, Application of clustering and text mining in financial problem solving. The course will be a practical hands-on course which would be delivered in excel/Python.
ho_4a95a8851c47.scope: This course aims at discussing the role of data and analytics in financial decision making, understanding the statistical properties of financial data. The student should be able to price different securities by understanding their characteristics and using different statistical and machine learning techniques. The student should also be able to create optimal portfolios catering to the requirements of different user groups and evaluate the portfolios using different metrics. ho_4d5a7c9d99b4.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.

ho_4d5a7c9d99b4.scope: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. ho_4eac3834b7e2.scope: Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc.

ho_5037b0fcc976.description: This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.

ho_518ae2f61b22.scope: Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math- ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc- tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design and analysis of algorithms.

ho_521b71dbe798.description: This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights from databases through data analytics powered by SQL.

ho_52c65bc5febe.scope: The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident, ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids. The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy, audience suitability, bias, and ethical use.

ho_57efe5c5ba6b.description: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. ho_57efe5c5ba6b.scope: The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. ho_5869b22f5e0d.description: Introduction to risk; types of risk; risk measurement; risk management techniques; risk avoidance, loss control, loss financing, risk retention, risk transfer, internal risk reduction through diversification etc.; insurance business and operations; insurance pricing; insurance v/s hedging; life, health and income risk; property and liability risk – commercial and personal; social insurance; insurance regulation 2 Scope and Objective of the Course: This course will examine the way in which business and society make an assessment of, control and transfer risk. The scope of this course is to provide a broad understanding of risk and insurance as a means to manage it. This forms the foundation to facilitate the students in their further studies on insurance. The course introduces the concept of risk and techniques of identifying, measuring and managing it. In this context, insurance as a risk management tool is discussed with references to its role, functions and basic principles as applicable to different classes of insurance. The objectives of the course are to provide students with  a comprehensive understanding for making risk management decisions to increase business value and individual welfare  a complete understanding of risk transfer through pooling and key features of insurance market  an understanding of the effects of and rationale for public policies that affect risk and its allocation  Knowledge about insurance markets and important details of an insurance contract as a risk management tool.  Assessing and evaluating insurance needs and implement effective solutions, involving and aligning the entire organization 3 Text Book: George Rejda and Michael McNamara ‘Principles of Risk Management and Insurance’ 14th edition, Pearson Education, 2022 (ISBN 9780134082578) 4 Reference Books:  John Teale, Insurance and Risk Management, CCH Australia Ltd, 2013  James Trieschmann, David Sommer, Robert Hoyt, Risk management and Insurance, Cengage Learning, 12 Edition, 2005  Harrington scott E.& Niehaus Gregory “Risk Management and Insurance” Tata McGraw-Hill, Second edition.2004 (or latest edition)  Scott E. ho_59b2de270114.scope: Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to veriﬁcation of signatures, and from analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of ﬁngerprints and human blood cells. Currently, pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces- sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.

ho_59fe52bbee89.description: This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices, viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth), dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti- yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.

ho_5a558532694b.scope: This course is designed to enrich theoretical, analytical as well as practical knowledge about metal cutting techniques and various machine tools used in manufacturing. The course include undrerstanding of important factors associated with machining such as what is the mechanics of cutting, why cutting fluid is necessary in metal removal, and how abrasive machining processes are different from tool-based cutting processes. The course also includes design aspect of cutting tools, machine parts (structure, spindles, jigs-fixtures) would be explored to comprehend the knowledge of machine tools.

ho_5b29aa5416f1.scope: The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures.

ho_5e2e4c44597c.description: This course studies the theory, design, and implementation of text-based information systems. The Information Retrieval core components of the course include statistical characteristics of text, representation of information needs and documents, several important retrieval models (Boolean, vector space, probabilistic, inference net, language modeling, link analysis), clustering algorithms, collaborative filtering, automatic text categorization, and experimental evaluation. The software architecture components include design and implementation of high-capacity text and multimedia retrieval and filtering systems.

ho_6119b030ce93.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology.

ho_6119b030ce93.scope: This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses.

ho_61d09573159c.description: This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

text: Make-up Policy: It will be given on extremely genuine grounds.

ho_61d09573159c.scope: A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems. Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

ho_63ca3d219b89.description: The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.

ho_64e2b47aab88.scope: In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.

ho_652633e4eb40.description: The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures. 2. Scope and Objective: The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors 3. Course learning outcomes: a. Explain the advantages of CORDIC in hardware implementation, especially in terms of multiplier-less architecture, low power, and area efficiency. b. Analyze the design principles of advanced VLSI processor architectures and their microarchitectural implementation strategies for high-performance computing systems. c. Evaluate various memory hierarchy designs and optimizations, including their microarchitectural aspects, in the context of different processor types. d. Apply concepts of parallelism—such as instruction-level, data-level, thread-level, and task-level parallelism—to optimize system performance. e.

ho_66220b5ca113.scope: International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.

ho_690006a70c2b.description: Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics). 2. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data. 3. CLO3: Apply principles of measurement, reliability, validity, scale development, and sampling to develop rigorous research instruments for social science investigations. CLO4: Analyze quantitative and qualitative data using appropriate statistical and qualitative analysis techniques, including the use of software such as SPSS, Jamovi, and NVivo. ho_69224e8e1613.scope: The objective is to develop knowhow and skills that promote human-centered approach to innovation through design thinking (DT). It will aim to develop understanding of consumer needs & using creativity for new ideas/products (or re-design products) for solving problems. Course will also help understand prototyping, testing of new ideas & see the context of the larger ecosystem. Focus will be on understanding design thinking concept and tools for effective innovations that can solve consumers’ needs holistically. Design Thinking process is laid across 3 stages- inspiration, ideation and implementation for new product development or re-design & concepts like MVP or minimum viable product, business model/canvas & business ecosystem will be also covered. The pedagogical focus will be on hands-on approach to learning.

ho_6d38c0bae327.description: Soft matter or soft condensed matter is a subfield of condensed matter comprising a variety of physical systems that are deformed or structurally altered by thermal or mechanical stress of the magnitude of thermal fluctuations. They include liquids, colloids, polymers, foams, gels, granular materials, liquid crystals, and biomolecules. These materials share an essential characteristic feature in that predominant physical behaviors occur at an energy scale comparable with room temperature thermal energy. At these temperatures, quantum aspects are less significant. In this course, our aim would be to understand the structure, properties, and dynamics of the soft matter. What is the order of forces and times scales that affect the overall behaviour of this class of matter?

ho_6e8648722cee.scope: The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of practical biology.
