ho_6f58255279c1.syllabus_text: Module 1: Vapor Power Cycles Learning Objectives  To analyze ideal Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate thermal efficiency by applying first law and second law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate performance of Rankine cycle considering isentropic efficiencies of turbine and pump.  To represent the Rankine cycle processes on the Mollier diagram (enthalpy•entropy chart).  To analyze reheat Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate its performance by applying first law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate performance of regenerative Rankine cycle using feed water heaters.  To study boilers their mountings and accessories. Learning Strategy: Topics Text book Chap/Sec Carnot cycle deficiencies, Simple vapor power cycle, Ranking Cycle, Actual vapor power cycle, Mean temperature of heat addition. Techniques for efficiency improvement, Reheat and Regenerative cycles with open & closed feed water heaters. Combined cycle power plant and its thermodynamics. Combined Heat and Power. 10, TB1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division Please do not print unless necessary Page 3 Module 2: Refrigeration Cycles Learning Objectives  To study simple refrigerators and heat pumps systems and the evaluate of their performance.  Analyze the ideal and actual vapor compression refrigeration cycle.  Evaluate the second law efficiency of vapor compression refrigeration cycle.  Introduce the concepts of vapor absorption-refrigeration systems.  To determine maximum COP of an ideal absorption refrigeration system. Learning Strategy: Topics Text book Chap/Sec Vapor Compression Refrigeration Cycle, Actual Vapor Compression Cycle, Heat Pump, Second Law Efficiency of Vapor Compression Cycle. 11, TB1 Basic principle of a Simple Vapour–Absorption System, Comparison of vapour compression refrigeration systems with continuous vapour absorption refrigeration systems, maximum COP of an ideal absorption refrigeration system, properties of ideal and real refrigerant-absorbent mixtures, single stage vapour absorption refrigeration system with solution heat exchanger. Introduction to compressors. 11; RB3 & RB4 Module 3: Psychrometry Learning Objectives  Differentiate between dry air and atmospheric air.  To define and calculate the specific and relative humidity of atmospheric air.  To calculate the dew-point temperature of atmospheric air and to relate the adiabatic saturation temperature and wet-bulb temperatures of atmospheric air.  To determine the properties of atmospheric air using psychrometric chart.  To apply the principles of the conservation of mass and energy to various air-conditioning processes.  To estimate heating and cooling loads of a space to be air conditioned. Learning Strategy: Topics Text book Chap/Sec Psychometric Properties, Psychrometric Chart, Mixing of moist air, Psychrometry of air conditioning processes. 14, TB1; RB3 & RB4 Inside and Outside Design Conditions, Simple Summer Air Conditioning System, Supply Air condition and flow rate, Apparatus Dew Point, Winter Air Conditioning. Building Cooling Load and Heating Load Estimate. 13 & 14, TB1; 30, RB3 & RB4 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division Please do not print unless necessary Page 4 Module 4: Gas Power Cycles Learning Objectives  To analyze Gas power cycles for a perfect gas using P•v and T•s plot and evaluate its performance using first law of thermodynamics.  To evaluate and compare the thermal efficiency of regenerative Stirling/Ericsson cycle with that of Carnot cycle.  To evaluate effects of multistage compression with intercooling, multistage expansion with reheat and regeneration on performance on a simple gas turbine cycle in terms of its efficiency.  To analyze combined cycle and binary cycle power plants using first and second law of thermodynamics and evaluate their thermal efficiency. Learning Strategy: Topics Text book Chap/Sec General introduction to Subject, Simple steam power plant, Internal Combustion Engines, Gas turbine plants, Refrigeration cycle and COP. Carnot Cycle, Air Standard Cycles, Otto Cycle, Diesel Cycle, Dual Cycle. Stirling cycle, Ericsson Cycle, Brayton cycle: intercooling, reheating and regeneration. Jet propulsion. Class notes 9, TB1 Module 5: Thermodynamic Relations Learning Objectives  To understand the Maxwell relations  To discuss the Clapeyron equation and understand its utility  Understanding the general thermodynamic relations and Joule Thomson effect. Learning Strategy: Topics Text book Chap/Sec Maxwell relations, Clapeyron Equation, Joule Thomson Coefficient and General Thermodynamic Relations. 12, TB1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division Please do not print unless necessary Page 5 Evaluation Scheme: Components Duration Weightage (%) Maximum Marks [200] Date & Time Remarks Quizzes (Best 3 out of 4) 45 min. 15 30 To be announced in class Closed book Mid-semester test 90 min. 25 50 07/10/2026 Closed book Lab Report, Quiz and Lab Examination ----- 25 50 To be announced in class - Comprehensive test 120 min. 35 70 08/12/2026 Open book Mid-semester grading: It will be announced normally in the month of November. The best 3 out of 4 quizzes will be considered for grading. The lab will cover experiments related to Applied thermodynamics. There will be separate marks awarded to lab reports for each experiment, comprehensive viva and quizzes will be conducted for the lab along with the final lab examination. Chamber Consultation Hours: Tuesday, 6-7 pm. Notices: All notices related to this course will be put on the Nalanda. Make-up Policy: It will be as per the institute rules. ho_70ead9b9ccf4.scope: The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathe- matical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built. The objectives of the course are: CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz method. CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer. CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid mechanics and heat transfer.

ho_7100bf33c22d.scope: The objective of the course is to introduce students to different types and forms of drama. In doing so, this course will familiarize students with various dramatic forms spanning different geographical spaces and time, thereby helping them to have a deeper understanding of the same. It will also enable the students to connect various dramatic forms through the study of visuals, timelines, and biographical and contextual readings that allow them to delve further into the history and conventions of the time period when these dramatic works were produced.

ho_74a82361df0d.scope: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas.

ho_7676c30ee445.scope: The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. ho_76a81492dac8.scope: This course details the various aspects and emerging concepts of operations management as they relate to the manufacturing/production function, maintenance, quality, and service operations. It provides a detailed view of each of the above functions, including their strategic importance, operational aspects, and roles in the supply chain. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: • This course will give students an overview of the various components of manufacturing and maintenance management as practised on the shop floor. The various kinds of manufacturing operations, the types of jobs performed, and the maintenance activities undertaken to ensure operational readiness and integration with other functions of the industry will be discussed. This will help one understand how the shop-floor execution and upkeep of resources (machines/equipment) are critical to the functioning of a coherent supply chain. • This will help the students to understand the importance of quality management. Explain the various quality management tools and techniques used in an organisation to ensure that quality products and services are produced. • This course will provide an overview of the service operations management. Customer service design, service operations and execution, and monitoring service delivery performance will be discussed.

ho_7770cd3e93fb.description: This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and numerous other applications. The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series, power series, Taylor and Maclaurin series, partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.

ho_77b4ace1b7c3.scope: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain. (R2) Fu, K. S., et al., Robotic: Control, Sensing, Vision & Intelligence, McGraw Hill ISE, 1987 (R3) Robert J., Schilling, Fundamentals of Robotics: Analysis and Control, Prentice Hall, NJ, 2002. ho_78465984cf24.description: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach. SCOPE and OBJECTIVES: Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES: The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. At the end of the course, student will be aware of many existing methods used to solve counting problems and when these methods are applicable. TEXT BOOK: T1: Alan Tucker, Applied Combinatorics, John Wiley & Sons, 6th Edition, 2012. T2: Allenby and Slomson, How to Count, CRC Press, 2nd Edition, 2011. REFERENCE BOOKS: R1. W.D. Wallis and J.C. George, Introduction to Combinatorics, CRC Press, 2th Edition, 2017. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 R2. Richard A. Brualdi, Introductory Combinatorics, Pearson, 4th Edition 2008. R3. Miklos Bona, Introduction to Enumerative Combinatorics, Tata McGraw-Hill, 2007. ho_79ade96b3950.description: This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions.

Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The zero-current- switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course.

ho_80418c4b3557.scope: People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability. The learning objectives of the course are as under:  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. ho_8303f089642d.scope: The objective of the course is to introduce the students with the microscopic description of the thermodynamics system and how macroscopic properties can be derived from microscopic description using statistical mechanics or statistical thermodynamics. In this course the statistical ensembles in classical mechanics, the concept of ensemble and phase space will help in understanding equilibrium statistical mechanics. Beyond this, this course will introduce the coding in either MATLAB or Python to do statistical analysis to find the thermodynamic or dynamic properties of the system. Several simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo Simulations and Molecular Dynamics using GROMACS and LAMMPS will be introduced to study applications of statistical thermodynamics to calculate various properties at nanoscale. • Course learning outcomes: a. Learning the fundamental concept of Statistical Thermodynamics b. Learning the concept of molecular dynamics simulation and Monte Carlo Simulation c. ho_83cfdd19f948.scope: The intent of the course is to present a broad undergraduate/post-graduate level introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP, a.k.a. computational linguistics), the study of computing systems that can process, understand, or communicate in human language. The primary focus of the course will be on understanding various NLP tasks as listed on the course syllabus, algorithms for effectively solving these problems, and methods for evaluating their performance. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: • To introduce students, the challenges of empirical methods for natural language processing (NLP) applications. • To introduce basic mathematical models and methods used in NLP applications to formulate computational solutions. • To provide students with the knowledge on designing procedures for natural language resource annotation and the use of related tools for text analysis and hands-on experience of using such tools. • To introduce students research and development work in information retrieval, information extraction, and knowledge discovery using different natural language resources. • To give students opportunities to sharpen their programming skills in neural networks (and deep learning) for computational linguistics applications.

ho_842b826b0d36.scope: This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignment multiple-access techniques (FDMA/TDMA/CDMA) and briefly explore random-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.
ho_842b826b0d36.syllabus_text: This undergraduate-level satellite communication course deals with the fundamentals of satellite communications. The course comprises six modules: M1) Module 1 consists of an introduction, historical developments, and research trends. M2) Module 2 covers satellite orbits, orbit elements, orbital effects, and Friendship7 spacecraft. M3) Module 3 comprises satellite link parameters, uplink, and downlink budget. M4) The fourth module consists of modulation, multiplexing, and error control coding. M5) The fifth module covers multiple access techniques. M6) The last module includes selected topics such as very small aperture terminal (VSAT), mobile sat (MSAT), the global positioning system (GPS), differential GPS (DGPS) and recent trends and advances. Module Description Reference CLO M1 L1–L2: Introduction, motivation, history, TRL, satellite segments & definitions. L3: Classify sample missions by TRL/segment Ch.1–TB CLO1 M1 L4–L5: Radio-wave propagation and frequency- selection effects. L6: Rain-fade/attenuation calculation Ch.8–TB CLO1, CLO2 M2 L7–L8: Orbits–LEO/MEO/GEO, merits/demerits, launch vehicles. L9: Orbital mechanics related concepts (se- lected) Ch.2,10,11–TB/RB1 CLO2 Continued on next page 2 Module Description Reference CLO M2 L10: Segments, space environment/physical medium. L11–L12: Spacecraft subsystems (power, telemetry, AOCS, sensors, thermal, propulsion). Ch.3–TB, RB2/RB3 CLO1 M2 L13: Subsystems continued. L14–L15: Communication payload/transponder (antenna, LNA, HPA–SSPA/TWTA). Transponder block-diagram design. Ch.3–TB, Ch.9–RB1 CLO1 M2/M3 L16: Reliability in satellite system design. L17–L18: RF link analysis intro–EIRP, G/T. Ch.3–TB, Ch.13– RB4, Ch.4–TB CLO1, CLO3 M3 L19–L21: Uplink/downlink C/N, C/N0, overall link budget. Preliminary link-budget design and examples Ch.4–TB, Ch.5–RB1 CLO3 M3 L22–L23: Intermodulation (IM), two-tone third-order IM. L24: IM noise concept, illustration, examples. Ch.6–TB CLO3 M4 L25–L27: Analog & digital signals, modulation and cod- ing schemes. Constellations and BER (reliability mea- sure). Ch.5,7–TB, RB2/RB3 CLO4 M4/M5 L28: Modulation/coding wrap-up. L29–L30: Multiple access–FDMA, TDMA. Ch.6–TB, Ch.6–RB1 CLO4 M5 L31–L32: CDMA; on-board/regenerative process- ing. L33: Capacity-comparison problems for FDMA/TDMA/CDMA. Review and other techniques Ch.6–TB, RB1 CLO4 M6 L34–L35: VSAT system planning & earth-station engi- neering. L36: VSAT network sizing, dependent parame- ters. Ch.9–TB CLO5 M6 L37–L38: Mobile satellite communication, non-GEO sys- tems, fading & remedies. L39: GPS/GNSS principles and receivers. Ch.10–TB, RB4 CLO5 M6/Selected Topics L40–L41: GPS/DGPS applications; L42–L43: Recent trends in SatCom Research articles (e.g., IEEE ComSoc) CLO5, CLO6

ho_8665784ba8ca.description: This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition.

text: Make-up Policy: Make-up will be given ONLY in extremely genuine cases; IC should be informed.

ho_8665784ba8ca.scope: Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology.

ho_87181e33e2c3.scope: This 4th level course introduces time series analysis and associated forecasting techniques, in which students will be equipped with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods for analyzing time series data. The course reviews extrapolative and decomposition models, introduction to Box–Jenkins time series analysis, and ARIMA models. The remainder of the course considers various practical aspects of the principles behind modern forecasting techniques. Students will study and develop the ability to select appropriate model to carry out forecasting. A one-hour lab will be conducted every week. Students will learn how to explore and analyze different types of time series data using R programming.

ho_871dc793a1b3.scope: The objective of the course is to introduce the students with the microscopic description of the thermodynamics system and how macroscopic properties can be derived from microscopic description using statistical mechanics or statistical thermodynamics. In this course the statistical ensembles in classical mechanics, the concept of ensemble and phase space will help in understanding equilibrium statistical mechanics. Beyond this, this course will introduce the coding in either MATLAB or Python to do statistical analysis to find the thermodynamic or dynamic properties of the system. Several simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo Simulations and Molecular Dynamics using GROMACS will be introduced to study applications of statistical thermodynamics to calculate various properties at nanoscale. • Course learning outcomes: a. Learning the fundamental concept of Statistical Thermodynamics b. Learning the concept of molecular dynamics simulation and Monte Carlo Simulation c. ho_872980e9e6b6.scope: This module is designed to provide students with solid technical knowledge and skills to build Internet of Things (IoT) systems. Internet of things has evolved due to convergence of multiple technologies - embedded systems, sensor technology, real-time data analytics, machine learning etc. Traditional fields of embedded systems, wireless sensor networks, control systems, automation (including home and building automation), and others all contribute to enabling the IoT. This course comprehensively covers various technologies and tools used for enabling IoT solutions. Knowledge of various topics required for building IoT prototypes like sensors and actuators/ Communications and networking and data management is also imparted in this course. This course would also help the students understand the various IoT security challenges and solution to address them. The course will also give the students exposure to how various real world problems are being solved by IoT based solutions (like in applications for smart city, smart farming etc.). There would also be some hands on sessions where students would learn how to build and program IoT systems and make end-to- end solutions for different applications. Furthermore, assignments and projects in this course would help students build IoT prototypes and apply what they have learnt in the course to solve real world problems.

Learning these concepts to understand how end to end IoT applications work. Module 2: Sensors and Actuators for IoT Lectures 5 - 8 Section 1.7, 15.4(T1), Chapter 7 (R4), relevant online resources Introduction to sensors for IoT application development, Data Acquisition, Signal Conditioning and Processing, Multi Sensor fusion for IoT, Advanced sensing techniques (e.g. BCI/HCI), Actuators and Controllers for IoT. Getting a hands on experience in these tools to enhance skill set. Module 4: Networking for IoT Lectures 18 - 23 Section 1.4.1 (R3), Chapter 7(R4), relevant online resources Understanding wireless sensor networks: Introduction, Deployment, Localization, Routing, MAC, Time synchronization and Multi-sensor-fusion for WSN. Blockchain fundamentals and it’s applications in IoT Module 5: Communications and networking in IoT Lectures 24-31 Chapter 16(T1) , Section 1.2.3 (T1), Section 12.4 (R4), relevant online resources Get an overview of Ad Hoc networks (MANET, VANET, FANET), Industrial IoT Networks, Common network standards (Bluetooth, NFC, LORA) etc, COAP and MQTT (including lab/ hands-on) Module 6: Data management in IoT Lectures 32-36 Section 1.5 (T1) , Chapter 5,6( R4), relevant online resources Understanding data management for IoT, Advanced optimization for processing sensor data, Machine learning for IoT data analytics, Introduction to IoT Cloud Services, Case studies of Cloud services for IoT and learning how to use them. Module 7: Security issues in IoT Lectures 37 - 40 Chapter 10, Section 1.8(T1), Chapter 10 (R4), relevant online resources Get an overview of cyber-attacks on IoT- Case study and understand security solutions for IoT: hardware/software BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3 Lab: Lab for the course would be in-class labs during the class hours when the relevant topics are covered. Labs would consist of hands on session where the students will learn how to work with microcontrollers and raspberry pi and learn building IoT applications from the scratch. Some of the suggested lab exercises are:  Programming Arduino/ Nodemcu (esp8266) microcontrollers.  Blinking LED using the above microcontrollers.  Interfacing sensors to microcontrollers.  Connecting microcontrollers to the internet and streaming sensor data to cloud.  Actuation using microcontrollers.  Raspberry pi programming and application development.  Rest API based hands on.  Lab exercise based on COAP/ MQTT.  IoT Security based labs

ho_8780b2604198.description: Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.

ho_883f2dddfb88.scope: Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges. This course will mainly focus on the design of three types of bridge superstructures namely Slab culverts/bridges, T-beam bridges, and Composite bridges. The design of the bridge substructure will include the design of elastomeric bearings and the design of abutments and piers. Moreover, the course will include the design aspects of continuous bridges. At the end of this course, the students would be equipped with the complete analysis and design of slab, T-beam and composite bridges, along with the design of substructures for them.

ho_88cdfa9b88ef.scope: This course is an introduction to the chemical reaction kinetics, design and performance of various types of chemical reactors for chemically reacting systems, which yield industrially important products. The emphasis in this course will be to understand the fundamentals of kinetics of homogeneous reactions, design and analysis of ideal reactors; and non-ideal flow.
ho_88cdfa9b88ef.syllabus_text: Module Lecture Objectives Textbook/ Reference Learning Outcomes M1 L1 Introduction: Scope and objectives of the course, methodology, concept of mole balances TB 1.1-1.2  History of reaction engineering and industrial examples of reactor  Fundamentals of chemical reaction engineering  Learn the techniques and algorithm of problem solving in reactor design L2-3 Mole balances: Different types of reactors, mole balances TB 1.3-1..5  Able to visualize different types of reactors and distinguish their application  Concept of general mole balance (GMB) in reaction engineering  Able to apply the GMB to different reactor  Derive the design equation in terms of molar flow rate M2 L4 Design equations: Conversion and reactor sizing TB 2.1-2.3  Able to define conversion in a reactor  Derive the Design equations for different types of reactors L5-8 Applications of design equations: Reactor sizing for batch and flow systems TB 2.4-2.6  Able to express reaction rate as a function of conversion, a number of reactors and reaction systems can be sized or a conversion calculated from a given reactor size  Arrange reactors in series to achieve the maximum conversion for a given Levenspiel plot M3 L9-11 Rate laws and stoichiometry: Basic definitions and stoichiometric tables TB 3.1-3.6  Able to write the rate law in terms of concentration and the Arrhenius temperature dependence.  Able to use the stoichiometric table to write the concentrations in terms of conversion to finally arrive at a relationship between the rate of reaction and conversion.  Able to should be able to connect and apply the concepts of mole balances, rate law, and stoichiometry) to study isothermal chemical reactions and reactors. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Page 3 of 6 M4 L12-13 Isothermal reactor design: Design structure, design of batch and flow reactors TB 4.1-4.4  Able to combine and evaluate the concepts of mole balances, rate law and stoichiometry to design the isothermal reactors  Able to design the batch reactor, CSTR, PFR, PBF, membrane reactor, and semi batch reactor.  Describe the effects of system variables such as particle size on the conversion  Able to solve the reaction engineering design problems: calculate volume, conversion, time etc. as required in design.  Able to diagnose and troubleshoot malfunctioning reactor L14 Effect of pressure: Pressure drop in reactors TB 4.5 L15 Mole balances in terms of concentration and molar flow rates: Mole balance on CSTRs, PFRs, PBRs and Batch reactors TB 4.7 M5 L16-18 Collection and analysis of rate data: Differential and integral methods of analysis, examples TB 5.1-5.5  Able to analyze data to determine the rate law and rate law parameters using the graphical and numerical techniques as well as software packages.  Able to perform Nonlinear regression to analyze rate-concentration data to determine the parameters, but the other techniques such as graphic differentiation help one get a feel for the disparities in the data  Should be able to carry out a meaningful discussion on reactor selection to determine the reaction kinetics along with how lo efficiently plan experiments. L19 Evaluation of laboratory reactors: Differential reactors, comparison of experimental reactors TB 5.6-5.7 M6 L20-22 Multiple reactions: Maximizing desired product in parallel and series reactions TB 6.1-6.3  Should be able to describe the different types of multiple reactions (series, parallel, complex, and independent) and to select a reaction system that maximizes the selectivity. The reader should be able to write down and use the algorithm for solving CRE problems with multiple reactions.  The reader should also be able to point out the major differences in the CRE algorithm for the multiple reactions from that for the single reactions, and then discuss why care must be taken when writing the rate law and stoichiometric steps to account for the rate laws for each reaction, the relative rates, and the net rates of reaction. Mid Semester Exam BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Page 4 of 6 M7 L23-24 Catalysis: Catalysts and mechanism of catalytic reactions TB 10.1-10.2  Able to discuss the steps in a heterogeneous reaction (adsorption, surface reaction, and desorption) and describe what is meant by a rate-limiting step.  Able to distinguish between molecular adsorption and dissociated adsorption should be explained by the student as should the different types of surface reactions (single site, dual site, and Eley-Rideal).  Given heterogeneous reaction rate data, one should be able to develop a rate law for Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics.  Because under a harsh environment catalysts do not maintain their original activity, one needs to define and describe the basic types of catalyst decay (sintering, fouling, coking, and poisoning).  In addition, one should be able to carry out calculations that predict conversion in the types of reactors (namely moving bed and STTR) used to offset the deactivation of the catalyst. L25-26 Finding the rate law: Mechanism, rate-limiting step and rate law TB 10.3 L27 Reactor design: Design of reactors for Gas-Solid reactions TB 10.4 M8 L28-31 Reactions in porous catalysts: Diffusion and reaction in porous catalysts TB 11.1-11.3 TB-12.1-12.4  Able to define and describe molecular diffusion and how it varies with temperature and pressure, the molar flux, bulk flow, the mass transfer coefficient, the Sherwood and Schmidt numbers, and the correlations for the mass transfer coefficient.  Able to choose the appropriate correlation and calculate the mass transfer coefficient, the molar flux, and the rate of reaction.  Able to describe the regimes and conditions under which mass transfer-limited reactions occur and when reaction rate limited reactions occur and to make calculations of the rates of reaction M9 L32-34 Non ideal reactors: RTD, measurement

ho_894b7cd24ce9.description: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and soft computing; Neural networks: Introduction, models, and its application in civil engineering, fuzzy logic and its application in decision making, Clustering; Genetic algorithms; Expert systems; Introduction to machine learning (Support Vector Machine), case studies. Scope and Objective: Artificial Intelligence (AI) may be considered a field of computer science that attempts to build technology to inculcate human cognition in computer systems, but applications are not limited to. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities. This course is structured to give an overview of the area, as well as some important soft computing techniques which are essential to solve the complex problems in terms of the fundamentals. The attributes of human intelligence such as reasoning, planning, learning etc. will be attempted to be understood to incorporate in problemsolving. Course learning outcomes: By the end of the course, the students should have a. Out of various techniques, emphasis will be on Genetic algorithm, Artificial Neural Network, and Fuzzy Systems a. General knowledge of the field of AI b. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve civil engineering problems. c. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter. d. Students will take up a group project/ term paper to study in detail the theoretical details of an intelligent system and implement that during the semester. Text books and references: TB1: Artificial Intelligence A Modern Approach; Stuart J.Russell, Peter Norvig, Third Edition Pearson Education, Inc., India TB2: Neural Networks, Fuzzy logic, and Genetic Algorithms Synthesis and Applications; S. Rajasekaran, G.A. Vijayalakshmi Pai, PHI Learning Pvt. Ltd, Delhi. Method of conduct of the course: The traditional method of teaching by chalk and board has been highly regarded for many educational levels. The chalk-and-board teaching system has been appreciated for creating an opportunity for direct and personal communication between teachers and students to engage with each other face to face. Approaches such as blended learning, collaborative strategies, and experiential learning promote engagement, critical thinking, and lifelong learning. Course Plan: weekly schedule for 16 weeks with [3] lectures per week Week no. Module Lect. no. Reference Learning Outcome

ho_89b7781ed7a9.description: This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources with special reference to its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement, and societal development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately productivity) of the employees can be enhanced.

ho_8a60bbfa3d88.scope: This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

ho_8aa0141bd2da.description: (Scope and Objective): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands. Text Book: I. Marketing Analytics (2026), 2nd ed. by Seema Gupta, Avadhoot Jathar. Wiley (recommended purchase). https://www.amazon.in/Marketing-Analytics-2ed-Seema- Gupta/dp/9373320483/ref=tmm_pap_swatch_0 Reference Book: I. Marketing Analytics: Based on First Principles (2022). Authors: by Robert W. Palmatier, J. Andrew Petersen, Frank Germann. Bloomsbury Academic India. II. Python for Marketing Research and Analytics. First Edition. Springer. Jason S. Schwarz, Chris Chapman, and Elea McDonnell Feit Session Plan S.No. Topic Chapter Number Learning Objectives

ho_8adcd19fae7a.scope: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.
ho_8adcd19fae7a.syllabus_text: Module No. Lecture Session Reference Learning Objectives (I): Introduction to Communication Systems and Bandwidth (2 Lectures) Lectures 1–2: Overview of the course; taxonomy of communication systems; block- level description of an end-to-end communication system; baseband and passband transmission; brief review of the Fourier transform and signal spectrum; signal bandwidth, channel bandwidth and bandwidth requirements in communication systems. T1: chapters 1, 2 Describe the functional blocks of an end-to-end communication system; distinguish between baseband and passband transmission; interpret communication signals in the time and frequency domains; and relate signal bandwidth to channel bandwidth. (II): Analog modulation and Demodulation (12 Lectures) Lectures 3–10: Amplitude-modulation techniques: DSB-SC, AM with carrier, SSB-SC, VSB; angle-modulation techniques: frequency modulation and phase modulation; bandwidth and power requirements; generation of AM and FM signals; Armstrong method of FM generation; and frequency-division multiplexing. T1: chapters 3,4 Explain frequency translation and the principles of amplitude and angle modulation; compare analog modulation schemes in terms of bandwidth and power requirements; describe methods for generating AM, FM and PM signals; and explain frequency-division multiplexing. Lectures 11–14: Synchronous detection; envelope detection; FM and PM demodulation; phase-locked-loop-based demodulation; and superheterodyne receivers. T1: chapter 3,4 Explain synchronous and envelope detection; describe FM- and PM-demodulation techniques, including PLL- based demodulation; and explain the architecture and operation of a superheterodyne receiver. (III) Communication Channels and Noise (10 Lectures) Lectures 15-19: Communication media and channel models; signal transmission over communication channels; conditions for distortionless transmission; amplitude and phase distortion; random variables and random processes; statistical averages; autocorrelation and power spectral density; Gaussian processes; bandpass random processes; sources and nature of noise; additive white Gaussian noise; and noise figure. T1: chapter 2,6,7 Explain communication-media and channel models; identify amplitude and phase distortion; apply random- variable and random-process concepts in communication- system analysis; interpret autocorrelation and power spectral density; and explain Gaussian noise, bandpass noise, AWGN and noise figure. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3 Lectures 20-24: Analog demodulation in the presence of additive noise; output signal-to- noise ratio; noise performance of AM, DSB-SC, SSB-SC, FM and PM receivers; threshold effect in angle modulation; and comparison of analog modulation systems under additive noise. T1: chapter 7 Analyse the effect of additive noise on analog demodulators; determine the output signal-to-noise ratio; compare the noise performance of amplitude- and angle-modulation systems; and explain the threshold effect in angle modulation. (IV): Digital Signal Representation, Modulation and Detection (12 Lectures) Lectures 25–29: Pulse modulation; quantisation and encoding; pulse-code modulation; delta modulation; baseband line-coding schemes, including NRZ, polar and Manchester signalling; power spectral density of line-coded signals; intersymbol interference; eye diagrams; Nyquist criterion for distortionless transmission; pulse shaping; and waveform representation of binary and M-ary passband modulation schemes, including ASK, PSK, QAM and FSK. T1: chapter 5, 8, 11 Explain digital representation using PCM and delta modulation; compare common line-coding schemes and their power spectra; analyse intersymbol interference using eye diagrams; apply the Nyquist criterion and pulse-shaping concepts; and interpret binary and M-ary digital-modulation waveforms. Lectures 30–36: Digital demodulation in the presence of additive noise; detection of digital signals in noise; optimum-threshold detection; probability of error and bit-error probability; matched filters and optimum receivers; and coherent and noncoherent detection of digital carrier-modulation schemes. T1: chapter 8, 9 Analyse the detection of digital signals in additive noise; determine optimum decision thresholds and bit- error probability; explain matched-filter and optimum- receiver principles; and compare coherent and noncoherent detection techniques. (V): Information Theory and Channel Coding (6 Lectures) Lectures 37-40 Measure of information; entropy; source coding; Shannon–Fano coding; Huffman coding; data compression; mutual information; channel capacity; capacity of the AWGN channel; Shannon’s theorem and fundamental communication limits; and digital-transceiver design considerations. T1: chapter 12 Explain the measures of information and entropy; apply source-coding and data-compression techniques; interpret mutual information and channel capacity; explain Shannon’s theorem and the capacity of an AWGN channel; and identify fundamental trade- offs in digital-transceiver design. Lectures 41-42 Error Detection and Correction Codes: Hamming codes; linear block codes; and an introduction to cyclic codes T1: chapter 13 Explain the principles of error detection and correction; apply basic Hamming and linear block codes; and describe the fundamental concept of cyclic codes. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4

ho_8bd5204cdbf3.scope: The objectives of this course are to provide the students with a fundamental understanding of Green Chemistry with an emphasis on the design, prepare and use of chemicals and protocols that have little or no pollution potential or environmental risk. Catalysis being considered as the prime tool to efficiently inculcate the ‘green’ aspects, will be discussed at length including its types, guiding principles and milestone applications. The students will get exposed to the latest development trends to obtain a comprehensive understanding.
ho_8bd5204cdbf3.syllabus_text: Modul e Lec. ho_8d4cc76cfcf6.description: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles. Scope and Objective of the Course: This course has been designed to make the students familiar with internal combustion engines and electric and hybrid electric power trains. Text Books: V. Ganesan, Internal Combustion Engines, Tata McGraw-Hill Pub. Co. Ltd, New Delhi, 4th Edition. Reference Books: 1. M.L. Mathur, R.P. Sharma, “A Course in Internal Combustion Engines”, Dhanpat Rai and Sons, New Delhi, 2005. 2. H.N. Gupta, “Fundamentals of Internal Combustion Engines”, Prentice Hall of India, 2nd Edition, 2013. ho_91ae1f639160.description: Review of Maxwell's equations; Wave propagation: Normal & Oblique incidence; Transmission Lines & Smith Chart, Waveguide: Rectangular & Cylindrical waveguides; Dielectric Waveguides; Cavity resonator, equivalent Circuit Model, characteristics; Microwave devices (Waveguide based and planar); S parameters; Measurement & Impedance Matching; Microwave Generators & Amplifiers; Antennas and its characteristics and types. Scope and objective of the course: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to analyze electromagnetic wave propagation using Maxwell’s equations, understand wave behavior at interfaces, and design transmission lines with impedance matching using the Smith Chart. They will gain proficiency in characterizing waveguides, cavity resonators, and microwave devices, as well as interpreting S- parameters for network analysis. Students will also learn measurement techniques, explore microwave sources and amplifiers, and evaluate various antenna types and their radiation characteristics for practical applications.

ho_95f3a22278a5.scope: A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure, intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental biology.

ho_9caf305a661c.description: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. Learning Objectives The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and geosphere. In addition to part I (General handout for all courses appended to the timetable) this portion gives further details regarding the course. Course No. : ENVS F212 Course Title : Environmental Chemistry and Environmental Biotechnology Instructor-in-charge and other instructor : Prof. Bibhas R. Sarkar (IC), and Prof. B. Vani Course Description: The course will provide an overview of the different aspects of the environment and the chemistry integrally involved in it. Broad description of the constituents of the environment namely the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, the geosphere and the anthrosphere (tangible human interaction space) will be provided with emphasis on the chemical interactions involved in each of them in their respective formation, balanced existence, deterioration (pollution and degradation/ depletion) and remediation processes etc. The course will be essential to gaining an understanding of our environment and the chemistry behind the processes occurring within, with relevance to the current industrialized ecology. The course will also provide an overview of environmental biotechnology, emphasising biotechnological tools, such as microbial, genetic, and biochemical mechanisms involved in ecosystem function, pollution, and remediation. The course will cover sustainable biotechnological interventions in waste treatment, bioenergy production, and pollution control. It is designed to build a foundational understanding of how biotechnology integrates with environmental systems, enabling learners to address environmental degradation in the context of modern industrialized ecology. Learning Objectives The course will be broadly divided based on the three major components as hydrosphere, atmosphere and geosphere. ho_9e7f01ab9b41.scope: This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines.

ho_9e89af02a92d.description: Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well- being of our planet.

ho_a0d64a113839.scope: This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. Scope: As an introductory course in Politics, this is based on lectures and reading texts. However, the students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 values. Most significantly, this Course facilitates students’ engagement with various political debates of contemporary India and the world.
ho_a0d64a113839.syllabus_text: Session 1-2 Themes Elements of the teaching-learning process: pedagogy and evaluation. Humanities and Social Sciences: Their subject matter and relevance. Why study politics? Terms in the title of the course Modern Political Concepts Sources & Studies Course hand-out. Class lecture. A brief reading on the etymology of ‘polis/politics’ Learning Outcomes Understand the nature of the course under study; the meaning and significance of Humanities and Social Sciences; and the terms in the title of the course. Session 3-5 Themes Politics: Subject-matter, nature of the discipline, and Politics as a master-art Sources & Studies Aristotle, Nicomahean Ethics, Bk. 1, chs. 1-3 and Bk. 10, ch.9. Learning Outcomes Appreciate the nature and scope of the discipline of Politics; its origins in the West; and its relation with ethics and rhetoric. Gain an acquaintance with the works of Aristotle, especially to detect how Aristotle’s ethics, politics and rhetoric are interconnected Session 6-8 Themes Morality in Politics; Machiavellian Sources & Studies Machiavelli, Prince and Skinner, Machiavelli: A very short introduction. BBC documentary on Machiavelli, Retrieved from https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wsMs-DuGy1o, 31 July 2019 Learning Outcomes To explain the Machiavellian revolution on the question of means versus ends in politics BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3 Session 9-10 Themes Thomas Hobbes and the social contract; ‘state of nature’ Sources & Studies Hobbes’ Leviathan, chs. XIII & XVIII; TB, ch. 1, pp. 11-17 Learning Outcomes To explain the concept of social contract according to Hobbes’ Leviathan Session 11-13 Themes John Locke and Two treatises of government; rights; government Sources & Studies Select passages from Locke’s Second treatise of government; TB, ch. 1, pp. 11- 17 and RB (1) ch. 13 on property especially the part on John Locke Learning Outcomes To explain the origins of the rights discourse and the role of govt. according to Locke Session 14-16 Themes Rousseau and the origins of inequality; social contract; general will; A critique of the social contract theory Sources & Studies Select passages from Discourse on the origins of inequality, pp. 31-36 Learning Outcomes To appreciate one of the most powerful Modern critiques of established political order/civilization (Rousseau) as well as understand the critique of the social contract philosophy Session 17-20 Themes State, nation, nationalism Sources & Studies TB ch. 2; RB (1) ch. 11; Anderson (1983) Gellner (1983) and Hobsbawm (1992) Learning Outcomes Understand the meaning, role, and functions of the State; Distinguish the State from Nation Session 21-23 Themes Forms of Government through the source of power: Democratic and Non- Democratic ones Sources & Studies Aristotle’s Classification of governments; Alan R Ball, Modern Politics and Government (Chapter 2) Learning Outcomes Understand the various forms of governments from classical to modern classification Session 24-27 Themes Civil Society Sources & Studies Charles Taylor, 1990, ‘Modes of civil society’, TB chp. 10 and RB chp. 8. Learning Outcomes Familiarize with the evolution of the concept of citizenship and the recent debates around it both national and global. Session 28-31 Themes Democracy Sources & Studies TB chapter 4; RB chapter 7; https://www.journalofdemocracy.org/articles/ BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 4 Learning Outcomes Understand the concept of democracy and various dimensions of it across the globe both as a form of government and as a way of life. Session 32-34 Themes Communism and Anarchism 19th century Contemporary Anarchism (anarchism as non-domination) Sources & Studies Andrew C Janos (1996) Some texts by Zerzan are available at johnzerzan.net Learning Outcomes Appreciate the anarchist critique of Modern civilization and contemporary society Session 35-38 Themes Maoism and Gandhism Sources & Studies Bhikhu Parekh (1989); https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-american-legacy-of- gandhi-11569643260 ; https://www.epw.in/journal/2020/25/perspectives/gandhi-and- pandemic.html?0=ip_login_no_cache%3Da3cd0a560d10cda56b380e4a2f66b 651 https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/23/opinion/how-mao-molded-communism- to-create-a-new-china.html ; https://www.nybooks.com/daily/2018/02/05/who-killed-more-hitler-stalin-or- mao/ ; Liu Kang (2015) Maoism: Revolutionary Globalism for the Third World Revisited Learning Outcomes Understand the two leaders who not just led their respective countries to emancipation but shaped the national identity Session 39- 40 Themes Secularism Sources & Studies RB Chapter 274; Jose Casanova’s article, ‘The Secular and Secularisms” Learning Outcomes Understand the concept of secularism, the historical context, and the debates around it in India Few sessions will be dedicated to oral presentations of written assignments by students. ho_a0db5b12c573.description: This course will discuss the physics behind the semiconductors and the devices. The structure of any solid material plays an important role in their operation; the discussion will start with basic crystal structures and will cover the quantum theory of solids. In the last part of the course, some special devices like solar cells, light emitting diodes etc. will be discussed.

ho_a2a7212e7de9.scope: In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover, management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and developed.

ho_a44fb6824683.scope: This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. The topics covered will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and optimization.

The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: ● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. ● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. ● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. ● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. ● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution. 2. ho_a7f09006d7bc.scope: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. This course will give the students an advanced understanding of the principles and mechanisms of the immune system and immune responses in the context of infection, malignancy and immunological disorders. The course will also enable the students to describe the fundamental mechanisms underlying immunologic disease and associate these mechanisms with strategies for therapeutic modulation of the immune system. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development.

ho_aa1154b769a1.description: Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis- tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re- alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter- pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference, analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R.

ho_acd3daed74db.scope: Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues to address and various approaches to choose from: Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.

ho_b30fa4de9b8a.description: Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.
