ho_b48e6eaa368f.scope: The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties, limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables. The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus Instruction Division _ Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques. ho_b5d88957a9ab.scope: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. ho_b607b3b4df7a.scope: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA).

ho_bc7dce7fa40f.description: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains.

ho_bdd553e12e4e.description: The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.
ho_bdd553e12e4e.scope: NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?

ho_c01f3de82567.description: [as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example.

ho_c0b77424d67c.scope: The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 ➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss t

ho_c2862fa0bc9b.description: This is a graduate level course on computer networking and assumes a student has a basic understanding of computer network concepts. This course is a topic-based course which primarily covers topics from Internet Architecture, Internet Congestion Control, Software Defined Networking, Delay Tolerant Networks, Wireless Networking, Quality of Service & Traffic Engineering, Network Performance & Management, Overlay Networks and Network Applications. Several research papers/articles/case studies will be discussed on different aspects of computer networking. This course will introduce students to the basic design principles on which today's Internet is based upon along with the current and emerging research topics in the computer networking area. In addition, this course will cover some recent proposals to improve network performance, functionality and scalability. This course will provide plenty of opportunity for learning by doing through projects, assignments and laboratory exercises.

ho_c46f5dc5f2d7.description: This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives.

ho_c846fc37595a.scope: Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on this scope, the following objectives have been listed:  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/ industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure, tall chimneys etc.  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.

ho_c906a61e2087.scope: This course is intended to a comprehensive knowledge of the technology related to Mechatronics and Automation. The necessity of integrating and embedding electronics and microprocessor into mechanical systems have been long felt, due to rapid progress in microprocessor computer based technology, in domestic products to manufacturing systems. Mechatronics is a recently defined engineering field that builds on the traditional mechanical engineering studies, combines it with technologies from the electrical, electronics, computer and control fields, using techniques such as simultaneous engineering to provide solutions in manufacturing applications. Also, mechatronics has been applied to manufacturing and other industrial automation: robotic automation found in car automated production lines, such as welding, and assembly line in computer integrated manufacture etc. Thus, the manufacturing system is greatly enhanced by the application of mechatronics. This course will develop overall background of the student in interdisciplinary mechatronic technology and a broad introduction to the issues encountered and techniques required in developing mechatronic products and automation systems.

ho_ca7f23690f68.scope: Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems have become well-established and are encountered in the physical sciences, engineering, economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems. This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.

ho_cc02f6730446.scope: This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial innovation.

ho_cc1e41832af1.scope: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. It then moves to the examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and outcomes. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.

The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. It emphasizes experimental design, hypothesis formulation, and experimental validation. It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems, documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration to ethical practices in experimentation.

ho_cd78f04354a8.scope: The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to: (i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali- bration, and uncertainty. (ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif- ferent domains. (iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational tools. (iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, and validation. (v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering principles. (vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen- tation and technical reporting. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2
ho_cd78f04354a8.title: Foundations of Measurements and Experimentation

ho_d0738f0c2e14.description: This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.

ho_d0738f0c2e14.scope: The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.

ho_d11bd7e86488.description: Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.

ho_d5e4fb05b347.scope: This course gives the basic understanding of Mechanical Operations, which involves size reduction, size separation, filtration, etc. and certain Mass Transfer Operations like humidification, drying, adsorption, membrane separation, and crystallization. ho_d64ae514fe47.description: This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.

ho_d64ae514fe47.scope: Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. ho_d790ef4665b3.description: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. ho_d855d514d96d.scope: The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 2 Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions.

ho_da951087f196.scope: This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.
ho_da951087f196.syllabus_text: Module No. Lecture Session Reference Learning Objectives (I): Introduction to Communication Systems and Bandwidth (2 Lectures) Lectures 1–2: Overview of the course; taxonomy of communication systems; block- level description of an end-to-end communication system; baseband and passband transmission; brief review of the Fourier transform and signal spectrum; signal bandwidth, channel bandwidth and bandwidth requirements in communication systems. T1: chapters 1, 2 Describe the functional blocks of an end-to-end communication system; distinguish between baseband and passband transmission; interpret communication signals in the time and frequency domains; and relate signal bandwidth to channel bandwidth. (II): Analog modulation and Demodulation (12 Lectures) Lectures 3–10: Amplitude-modulation techniques: DSB-SC, AM with carrier, SSB-SC, VSB; angle-modulation techniques: frequency modulation and phase modulation; bandwidth and power requirements; generation of AM and FM signals; Armstrong method of FM generation; and frequency-division multiplexing. T1: chapters 3,4 Explain frequency translation and the principles of amplitude and angle modulation; compare analog modulation schemes in terms of bandwidth and power requirements; describe methods for generating AM, FM and PM signals; and explain frequency-division multiplexing. Lectures 11–14: Synchronous detection; envelope detection; FM and PM demodulation; phase-locked-loop-based demodulation; and superheterodyne receivers. T1: chapter 3,4 Explain synchronous and envelope detection; describe FM- and PM-demodulation techniques, including PLL- based demodulation; and explain the architecture and operation of a superheterodyne receiver. (III) Communication Channels and Noise (10 Lectures) Lectures 15-19: Communication media and channel models; signal transmission over communication channels; conditions for distortionless transmission; amplitude and phase distortion; random variables and random processes; statistical averages; autocorrelation and power spectral density; Gaussian processes; bandpass random processes; sources and nature of noise; additive white Gaussian noise; and noise figure. T1: chapter 2,6,7 Explain communication-media and channel models; identify amplitude and phase distortion; apply random- variable and random-process concepts in communication- system analysis; interpret autocorrelation and power spectral density; and explain Gaussian noise, bandpass noise, AWGN and noise figure. BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division 3 Lectures 20-24: Analog demodulation in the presence of additive noise; output signal-to- noise ratio; noise performance of AM, DSB-SC, SSB-SC, FM and PM receivers; threshold effect in angle modulation; and comparison of analog modulation systems under additive noise. T1: chapter 7 Analyse the effect of additive noise on analog demodulators; determine the output signal-to-noise ratio; compare the noise performance of amplitude- and angle-modulation systems; and explain the threshold effect in angle modulation. (IV): Digital Signal Representation, Modulation and Detection (12 Lectures) Lectures 25–29: Pulse modulation; quantisation and encoding; pulse-code modulation; delta modulation; baseband line-coding schemes, including NRZ, polar and Manchester signalling; power spectral density of line-coded signals; intersymbol interference; eye diagrams; Nyquist criterion for distortionless transmission; pulse shaping; and waveform representation of binary and M-ary passband modulation schemes, including ASK, PSK, QAM and FSK. T1: chapter 5, 8, 11 Explain digital representation using PCM and delta modulation; compare common line-coding schemes and their power spectra; analyse intersymbol interference using eye diagrams; apply the Nyquist criterion and pulse-shaping concepts; and interpret binary and M-ary digital-modulation waveforms. Lectures 30–36: Digital demodulation in the presence of additive noise; detection of digital signals in noise; optimum-threshold detection; probability of error and bit-error probability; matched filters and optimum receivers; and coherent and noncoherent detection of digital carrier-modulation schemes. T1: chapter 8, 9 Analyse the detection of digital signals in additive noise; determine optimum decision thresholds and bit- error probability; explain matched-filter and optimum- receiver principles; and compare coherent and noncoherent detection techniques. ho_dbf58fb37270.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. ho_de2167566656.scope: The chemical industry has undergone significant changes during the past 25 years due to the increased cost of energy, increasingly stringent environmental regulations, and global competition in product pricing and quality. One of the most important engineering tools for addressing these issues is optimization. Optimization as the name suggests, deals with finding the optimum design parameters for maximizing the profit or minimizing the total investment on a process plant. The criteria for analysis of the economic objective function involve fulfilling a process criteria restrictions, conditions, design equations, and respecting the limits of the variables. Most problems in chemical engineering processes have many solutions, in some cases becoming endless. The optimization is related to the selection of an option that is best in a variety of efficient options but being the only one that comes closest to an economic optimum performance and operation. This course, as a subject, deals with the concepts of modeling & simulation, various methods of optimization, objective functions, constraints, theoretical & computational basis for optimization techniques, various chemical engineering examples, etc. The objective of the course is to apply the optimization techniques in chemical engineering processes for reducing the operating cost and maximizing the profit. After completing this course the students will be able to apply the principle of optimization in solving engineering problems and understand the scope of optimization in solving Chemical Engineering problems.

ho_e1b7bfb3d3d2.scope: This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.

ho_e447a93c1243.description: This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.

ho_e447a93c1243.scope: Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.

ho_e55f7241a193.scope: Transport phenomena is one of the basic subjects of chemical engineering and includes study of fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer. The governing equations for the aforementioned transport processes are analogous in nature as the underlying molecular mechanisms are very closely related. The objective of this course is to cover advance topics in this area like the transport of momentum, heat and mass in turbulent flow, creeping flows, flow through porous media, flow over flat plates and curved surfaces, interphase transport, etc. A balanced overview and fundamental equations for transport processes would be provided along with illustrations regarding solving relevant problems. Further, some special cases which are frequently encountered would also be covered.

ho_e562df5c4053.scope: In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price- cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. With a market capitalization greater than the value of General Motors, Ford and Chrysler combined; Toyota is the world’s most profitable automaker. Toyota’s well known “secret weapon” is lean manufacturing – the revolutionary approach to business processes that it invented in the 1950’s and has spent decades for perfecting. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? The course explains Toyota’s unique approach to Lean manufacturing, that drive Toyota’s quality and efficiency obsessed culture. You will valuable insights that can be applied to any organization and any business process, whether in services or manufacturing. You will discover how the right combination of long- term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. At the end of this course, the students will be able to understand the importance of lean manufacturing / The Toyota Way as a strategic weapon, the students will be able to understand the World –Class power of the Toyota way

ho_e8759efd1da1.description: Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along

ho_e8759efd1da1.scope: This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. ho_eca54e03dcab.scope: The main objective is to learn how to use mathematical and statistical methods in economics. It involves a review of the fundamentals of mathematics and statistics, which can be used in applied economics. Knowledge of these fundamentals and their application in applied economics would help students better understand the entire economic system and the policymaking process. At the end of this course, students will be able to understand and solve graduate-level problems in economics and finance using the knowledge they have gained. Specifically, this course uses fundamentals from calculus, algebra, optimization, and basic statistics. This course would lay the foundation for students to understand related courses in economics and finance, such as econometrics and growth theory.

ho_ed44c1767325.scope: A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera- tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute- force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in- cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis. Objectives • Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob- lems. • Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority queues) for complex applications. • Use algorithmic techniques (brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming) to address real-world challenges. • Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.

ho_f11b268edbf0.scope: The course aims to cover topics in advanced areas of organic chemistry. The focus will be on the application of structure and theory to the study of organic reactions: nucleophilic aromatic substitution, organometallic reagents in organic synthesis, reaction dynamics, isotope effects, and molecular orbital theory applied to pericyclic and photochemical reactions; reactive intermediates including carbenes, carbanions, and benzyne; and asymmetric synthesis and multistep synthesis using the disconnection approach. Starting with fundamental principles and their application, the ultimate purpose of this course will be to understand the recent developments in organic chemistry.

ho_f166315c5b7f.scope: The course is designed in consideration to growing the basic level knowledge and understanding in inorganic chemistry. It includes electronegativity, detailed study of acid-base chemistry, non-aqueous solution chemistry, concept of redox chemistry, shape and structure of inorganic covalent molecules using VSEPR model and bonding of ionic compounds in solid state. It includes the chemistry of halogen and noble gases and main group elements. There will have thorough discussion of chemistry of macromolecules containing inorganic chains, rings and cages.This course will attempt to provide the students with sufficient basic knowledge of the structure and reactivity of inorganic systems to ensure a more comprehensive understanding. By the end of semester, you will be able to learn – ➢ Different scales to define electronegativity; rationalization of unusual reactivity ➢ Shape and structure of different covalent molecules and ionic compounds ➢ Measures of acid-base strength in gas and solution phase; Relation between hardness and softness, Symbiosis ➢ Chemistry of protonic and aprotic solvents; Redox stability; Diagrammatic presentation of potential data ➢ Use (or not) of d orbitals by nonmetals; Reactivity and d orbital participation ➢ Positively charged halogens; Pseudohalogens ➢ Numerous examples in nature of inorganic chains, rings and cages – their structures and chemistry

ho_f629581e3f13.description: This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.

ho_f629581e3f13.scope: The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. ho_f672158e9d53.scope: The course’s main objective is to provide students with a firsthand experience of basic techniques used in an organic chemistry laboratory. Broadly, the experiments include qualitative organic analysis, detection of known and unknown functional groups, chemical separation of a mixture of two compounds, examples of single-step and two-step organic syntheses, extraction of organic compounds from natural sources or from drugs, chromatographic separation of the pure compound from a mixture obtained in a multistep reaction, etc.
ho_f672158e9d53.syllabus_text: The students will perform several experiments in qualitative, synthetic organic chemistry, including single- step and multi-step synthesis, extraction of natural products, and training in chromatographic separation, with an emphasis on individual planning and execution of the experiments. The students will be divided into two sections (I & II), and each section will conduct a set of experiments (Lab I or Lab-II experiments) in the first half semester, and thereafter, interchanging of the students will proceed during the second half of the semester. Selected 20 experiments will be discussed and performed in the class. ho_f6c8b0dba33e.description: Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.

ho_f6c8b0dba33e.scope: The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.

Module 2: Urban Water Supply and Sanitation Week 3–5 [L7-15] TB1, TB2 - Explain water sourcing, distribution systems, and recycling strategies. - Evaluate water quality parameters and understand testing and treatment technologies. - Understand fundamentals of sanitation, sewerage, and urban drainage design. Module 3: Stormwater and Groundwater Management Week 6–8 [L16-24] TB1, TB2 - Analyze stormwater drainage systems and sustainable urban drainage systems (SUDS). - Design recharge and rainwater harvesting systems in urban areas. - Examine groundwater challenges and risk management in urban contexts. Module 4: Sustainable Design and Decision Tools Week 9–10 [L25-L30] TB1, TB2 - Apply water-sensitive urban design principles and sustainability indicators. - Understand fundamentals of asset management and GIS applications in water systems. Module 5: Software Applications and Advanced Topics Week 11– 14 [L31-L42] USEPA, journal papers - Use modeling tools for urban stormwater and flood management (e.g., SWMM, HEC- RAS). - Apply hydroinformatics tools for advanced systems performance assessment. - Evaluate the effects of urbanization and climate change on urban water systems. - Synthesize learning through case studies and project-based assessments. ho_f7b01cf159ae.description: The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed.

ho_f7b823046ccb.scope: The primary objective of the course is to introduce the student to cloud computing from architectural and design perspectives. As such, the emphasis of the course would be on the underlying infrastructure and architecture of clouds, techniques for enabling services and the quality of such services, as well as issues in designing clouds. Select research issues in performance, security, and management would also be addressed. Programming on the cloud would be encouraged but not taught in class. Students are expected to learn and understand tools and techniques for using, designing, and implementing clouds and services via assignments and a term project. 2. Text Book T1. None 3. Modules Module Theme Learning Objectives I Cloud Computing – Introduction ● Learn how computing evolved over decades ● Learn cloud computing definition and its defining characteristics. ● Learn the service delivery models, deployment models ● Learn economic aspects of Cloud Computing ● Economic models and SLAs II Cloud Infrastructure ● Learn the hardware building blocks of a cloud datacenter (compute, storage and network) ● Learn energy and power efficiency of cloud datacenter ● Learn workloads and software infrastructure in a cloud datacenter III Virtualization ● Learn about process VMs and System VMs ● Learn the approaches to virtualize (classical, software-assisted, para-virtualization, hardware-assisted) ● Learn how to virtualize CPU, Memory, and I/O in all three approaches using case studies (VMWare, Xen, Intel VT-x) ● Learn about Linux Containers ● Learn about Namespaces, Control Groups, Capabilities ● Explore LXC and Docker IV Cloud Storage ● Learn about storage models, file systems and databases ● Learn cloud storage concepts (consistency, replication, consensus) ● Learn about large scale distributed file systems (GFS, HDFS, Ceph FS) ● Learn about cloud databases (Dynamo DB) and explore HBase, MongoDB, Cassandra. ● Learn about cloud object storage (Amazon S3) and explore OpenStack Swift, Ceph. V Programming Models ● Learn the concepts of distributed programming for the Cloud ● Learn batch processing programming model (Hadoop MapReduce) ● Learn programming model for iterating and interactive applications (Spark) ● Learn programming model for stream processing (Storm) VI Cloud Management, Performance and Security Issues ● Learn about SLAs, SLOs, availability, scalability, and elasticity ● Learn the principles and techniques in scaling services and building them ● Learn about software defined networking and storage in Cloud Data centers (Openstack) ● To understand performance issues and techniques to enable performance of a cloud at different levels of abstraction ● To understand security issues specific to cloud computing and solutions to address them. b. ho_faa0eca675d0.description: The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

ho_fde114d66c07.scope: Reconfigurable (adaptive) computing is a novel yet important research field investigating the capability of hardware to adapt to changing computational requirements such as emerging standards, late design changes, and even to changing processing requirements arising at run-time. Reconfigurable computing thus benefits from a) the programmability of software similar to the Von Neumann computer and b) the speed and efficiency of parallel hardware execution.The purpose of the course reconfigurable computing is to instruct students about the possibilities and rapidly growing interest in adaptive hardware and corresponding design techniques by providing them the necessary knowledge for understanding and designing reconfigurable hardware systems and studying applications benefiting from dynamic hardware reconfiguration.

ho_fe38cd468ab1.description: This elective course introduces the fundamental principles and emerging applications of microfluidics. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical insights relevant to microscale fluid behavior, fabrication methods and devices. Scope and Objective of the Course: The scope of this course spans across fundamental science, device engineering, and emerging real-world applications at the micro- and nano-scale. This course provides a comprehensive understanding of microscale fluid dynamics, and control principles central to microfluidic systems. The course objectives are to understand the basics of microfluidics and the physics governing microfluidic flows and interfaces, to explore various microfabrication techniques suitable for fluidic devices and to analyze and understand the microfluidic systems applications in various engineering domains. ho_fee1e91c5b39.scope: This course includes the analysis of polymers and biopolymers at a molecular scale, and design of devices used in contact with biological systems. Topics include molecular interactions between bio- and synthetic molecules and surfaces; design, synthesis, and processing approaches for materials that control cell functions; and application of state-of-the-art materials science to problems in tissue engineering, drug delivery, vaccines, and cell-guiding surfaces. This course covers the fundamental concepts (physical chemistry, chemistry, and materials physics, and biology) behind the design at a molecular scale of synthetic materials with biological functions.
